title: Ellsworth radar-jet chase and Bismarck lights
place_text: Ellsworth AFB, South Dakota and Bismarck, North Dakota

tellings.quote: On August 5th, 1953, a trained civilian spotter calls into the base.
The initial incident in this chain of UFO sightings was the sighting by a GOC (Ground Observers Corps) observer of a stationary "red glowing light" at 2005 LST near Blackhawk, S. Dak.
The report was relayed to the Rapid City Filter Center, and three airmen from the radar site were sent outside to look for the UFO.

An F-84 fighter was vectored in to a stationary blip near Blackhawk, and the pilot "chased" a UFO which he found at the location on a heading of 320 ° M. without gaining on it. The F-84 was probably chasing a star, in this case Pollux (mag. 1.2) which was in the correct location (335° true azimuth, near the horizon).

In summary, the Rapid City-Bismarck sightings appear to have been caused by a combination of: stars seen through an inversion layer, at least one meteor, AP echoes on a GCI radar, and possible ghost echoes on the GCI radar and malfunction of an airborne radar gunsight (although the commanding officer of the Rapid City detachment was later skeptical that there had in fact ever been even a ghost echo present on the GCI radar).

plain: On a night in August 1953, glowing lights over South Dakota and North Dakota are said to have been tracked on radar and chased by a jet fighter from Ellsworth Air Force Base, with more lights seen over Bismarck. Michels tells it from Project Blue Book, the US Air Force's UFO study of the 1950s and 60s, and from its one-time head, Edward J. Ruppelt: "On August 5th, 1953, a trained civilian spotter calls into the base." The case was also studied by the researcher Gordon D. Thayer in the Condon report, a University of Colorado study of UFO reports published on 31 October 1968. That report begins with an observer from the Ground Observer Corps, civilian volunteers who watched the skies, who saw a stationary "red glowing light" near Blackhawk. It says the report "was relayed to the Rapid City Filter Center", a reporting hub, rather than called into the base, and that airmen went outside to look. It says an F-84 fighter chased the light "without gaining on it" and "was probably chasing a star, in this case Pollux". It sums up the case as stars seen through a warm layer of air, at least one meteor, and false radar echoes. The report notes, though, that the commanding officer doubted there had ever been even a false echo. The report gives a reading that differs from Michels's account, while his Blue Book record is not quoted. If the lights were not stars, military radar and a pilot would have tracked something unknown over American bases.

discussion.by: Scientific Study of Unidentified Flying Objects (the Condon report, 1968)
discussion.text: The teller credits Project Blue Book without naming a record; the Blue Book case file is on Wikimedia Commons only as a scan and is not read here. The Condon report's analysis of the case (Case 15-B) says the Ground Observer Corps observer's report was relayed to the Rapid City Filter Center rather than called into the base, and puts the sightings down to stars seen through an inversion layer, at least one meteor and anomalous radar echoes.
